newsitem.title: UK: British court says asylum seekers due state aid.
newsitem.headline: British court says asylum seekers due state aid.

text.p: A High Court judge ruled on Tuesday that asylum seekers must be given basic state aid while their claims for refugee status are being considered by Britain.
In a ruling challenging government regulations introduced in July to crackdown on bogus asylum seekers, the judge said refugees were entitled to "the basics for survival".

"I find it impossible to believe that parliament intended that an asylum seeker, who was lawfully here and who could not be lawfully removed from the country, should be left destitute, starving and at risk of grave illness and even death because he could find no one to provide him with the bare necessities of life," Judge Paul Collins said in his judgment.
He was ruling on a test case brought by four asylum seekers from Iraq, Romania, Algeria and China who have been refused housing by local councils in London.
The Algerian was found sleeping in a London park eating food left out for birds before he was taken in by a charity.

The councils were acting on new rules -- described by opponents as "the most draconian piece of legislation this century" -- which say refugees will get state aid only if they make formal applications for asylum as sooon as they enter Britain.
The councils were given the right to appeal the judgment but charities helping refugees hailed the ruling as a victory.
The Refugee Council estimates that some 8,000 people are currently seeking asylum in Britain with no entitlement to state aid or the right to work.

"What the courts have said today is that they are not prepared to see people who come from abroad -- genuine asylum seekers -- starving to death on the streets of Britain," Jerry Clore, lawyer for the four, said.
Opposition Liberal Democrat spokesman Lord Conrad Russell said the judgment had come just in time to save asylum seekers from "freezing on the streets" this winter.
Britain's Conservative government believes that the vast majority of those seeking asylum in Britain are not genuine refugees but economic migrants.
About 25 percent of applicants are given permission to remain in the country. The remaining 75 percent refused are regarded as people coming to Britain merely to seek a better life.
